newsitem.title: USA: Mistic owner buys Snapple from Quaker for $300 million.
newsitem.headline: Mistic owner buys Snapple from Quaker for $300 million.

text.p: Triarc Companies Inc., owner of the Mistic and Royal Crown soft drink brands, said Thursday it agreed to buy Quaker Oats Co.'s troubled Snapple drinks unit for $300 million in cash.

Snapple's ready-to-drink teas and juice drinks are a leader in the premium beverage market, with 1996 sales of about $550 million, but the unit has lost money since Quaker bought it on Dec. 6, 1994, for $1.7 billion.
In a separate statement, Quaker said it would take a non-cash pretax charge of about $1.4 billion, or $8.40 per share, in its first fiscal quarter, to record the loss on the sale.
It said it would be able to recoup about $250 million in taxes paid on previous capital gains, "making the cash value of the transaction approximately $550 million."
"The decision to sell Snapple was reached after an extensive review of various shareholder value-building options by management ...," Quaker Chairman William D. Smithburg said in a statement.

"After reviewing all possible options, we decided it was in the shareholders' interest to remove the financial burdens and risks Snapple brought to the portfolio and better focus on our value-driving businesses."
Triarc said it expected to close the deal by the end of June, subject to customary closing conditions, including government antitrust clearance.

New York-based Triarc, whose businesses include Royal Crown Co. and Mistic Brands Inc., fast-food restaurant Arby's Inc., liquefied petroleum gas company National Propane and specialty dyes and chemicals maker C.H. Patrick, has annual revenues of nearly $1 billion.
Quaker, known for its cereals and other prepared foods, also owns Gatorade sports drink.
"Last year, U.S. and Canadian foods and Gatorade delivered operating income in excess of $500 million. These businesses continue to perform well," Smithburg said.
Quaker said that as a result of the sale, its earnings -- excluding the one-time loss -- were expected to increase by about 10 cents a share in 1997 as debt is reduced and Snapple losses removed.
Quaker's board had previously rejected shareholder proposals that the Chicago-based food giant separate its beverage unit from its core food businesses.
Quaker's stock, which closed Wednesday at $37.50 Wednesday, did not immediately begin trading when the the New York Stock Exchange opened Thursday.
